title: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) Organises Scientific Conclave on Advancing Quality, Safety and Innovation in Drugs and Phytopharmaceuticals at NIPER Guwahati
subtitle:
IPC Launches Seven Indian Pharmacopoeia Phytochemical Reference Standards and Five Botanical Reference Standards
First Scientific Conclave in Northeast Brings Together Regulators, Academia and Scientific Institutions to Advance Phytopharmaceutical Standardisation
Initiative to Strengthen Scientific Standardisation, Quality Assurance and Evidence-Based Development of Plant-Based Medicinal Products
body_text:
The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC), under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, Government of India, organised a Scientific Conclave and Interactive Session on “Indian Pharmacopoeia (IP) 2026: Advancing Quality, Safety, and Innovation in Drugs, Food and Phytopharmaceuticals” at the National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research (NIPER) Guwahati on 27 th August 2026.
The interactive meeting, organised for the first time in the Northeast region, brought together experts and stakeholders from regulatory authorities, academia and scientific institutions to deliberate on the way forward for strengthening the quality and standardisation of phytopharmaceuticals in the country.
A major highlight of the event was the launch of seven Indian Pharmacopoeia Phytochemical Reference Standards (IPPRS) and five Indian Pharmacopoeia Botanical Reference Standards (IPBRS) by IPC, marking the first-ever introduction of these critical reference standards by the Commission. The standards launched are Andrographolide, Capsaicin, Embelin, Eugenol, Marmelosin/ Imperatorin, Scopoletin, Umbelliferone, Terminalia arjuna, Bacopa monnieri, Tinospora cordifolia, Centella asiatica, Ocimum sanctum.
Phytopharmaceuticals represent an important interface between traditional medicinal knowledge and modern scientific approaches, facilitating the development of safe, effective and standardised plant-based medicines. They have the potential to contribute to drug discovery, affordable healthcare and India's growing contribution to the global pharmaceutical sector.
The launch of the IPPRS and IPBRS marked a significant advancement in the scientific standardisation, quality assurance and regulatory evaluation of plant-derived medicinal products. The reference standards are expected to support the evidence-based development, quality control and therapeutic evaluation of phytopharmaceuticals, thereby strengthening their scientific and regulatory foundation.
The standards were launched by Prof. Ashok Puranik, Executive Director, AIIMS-Guwahati, who also addressed the gathering on the occasion. He described the initiative as a remarkable step towards strengthening the quality, safety and scientific validation of herbal and plant-based medicinal products.
In his inaugural address, Dr. V. Kalaiselvan, Secretary-cum-Scientific Director, Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, highlighted the importance of collaboration with the NIPER Guwahati laboratory in ensuring robust quality standards for phytopharmaceuticals. He emphasised that such collaborative efforts are crucial for advancing scientific standardisation and promoting quality-assured plant-based medicinal products.
The event was also graced by Dr. B. Kumar, DDC(I), CDSCO (EZ), and Dr. Ethengbemo Ezung, ADC, Nagaland, along with experts and stakeholders from the regulatory, academic and scientific communities.
The meeting provided an important platform for interaction among experts from regulatory authorities, NIPER Guwahati and IPC, with a focus on promoting evidence-based medicines derived from medicinal plants. The initiative is expected to strengthen the availability of safe, effective and affordable plant-based therapeutic options while encouraging further research, innovation and scientific advancement in the field of herbal and phytopharmaceutical medicines.

ministry.name: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare

enrichment.summary: The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) held its first Northeast scientific conclave on phytopharmaceuticals at NIPER Guwahati on 27 August 2026, bringing together regulators, academia and scientific institutions. At the event, IPC launched its first-ever seven Indian Pharmacopoeia Phytochemical Reference Standards (IPPRS) and five Indian Pharmacopoeia Botanical Reference Standards (IPBRS), covering compounds like Andrographolide, Capsaicin and Eugenol, and plants like Tinospora cordifolia and Ocimum sanctum. The initiative aims to strengthen scientific standardisation and quality assurance of plant-based medicines.
enrichment.context:
The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission, under the Ministry of Health and Family Welfare, is the statutory body responsible for setting standards for drugs sold in India, publishing the Indian Pharmacopoeia and providing reference substances used to test drug quality. India has been pushing to scientifically validate and standardise its vast traditional and herbal medicine base (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani) so that phytopharmaceuticals can be integrated into mainstream evidence-based healthcare and made globally competitive, in line with CDSCO's phytopharmaceutical drug regulatory pathway introduced in 2015. Reference standards are essential benchmarks used by laboratories to verify the identity, purity and potency of herbal ingredients and formulations, addressing long-standing concerns about adulteration and inconsistent quality in herbal products.

This conclave, the first such IPC event in the Northeast—a region rich in biodiversity and traditional medicinal plant knowledge—signals an effort to decentralise standardisation activities and involve regional institutions like NIPER Guwahati and AIIMS Guwahati. While the launch of new reference standards is a genuine regulatory/scientific milestone for phytopharmaceutical quality control, it is an incremental addition to IPC's ongoing standard-setting mandate rather than a new policy or law.

prelims_questions.question: The Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) functions under which Ministry of the Government of India?
options: Ministry of Health and Family Welfare
prelims_questions.explanation: The release states IPC operates under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare, and is responsible for setting drug quality standards including reference standards.

prelims_questions.question: What is the primary purpose of 'Reference Standards' such as the Indian Pharmacopoeia Phytochemical Reference Standards (IPPRS) mentioned in the release?
options: To fix the market price of herbal drugs
To serve as benchmarks for verifying identity, purity and quality of pharmaceutical/phytochemical substances
To register patents for medicinal plants
To regulate export duties on herbal products
prelims_questions.explanation: Reference standards are used in quality control and regulatory evaluation to verify identity, purity and potency of drug substances, as highlighted in the release.

mains_questions.question: Discuss the significance of standardisation and quality assurance in mainstreaming phytopharmaceuticals within India's healthcare and pharmaceutical regulatory framework.
Examine the role of institutions like the Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission in bridging traditional medicinal knowledge with modern scientific and regulatory standards.

study_notes.reason: The release's core value lies in factual details about IPC's statutory role and the newly launched reference standards, which are the kind of testable institutional/scheme facts UPSC favours; the analytical angle (mainstreaming traditional medicine) is present but thin and secondary here.

prelims.point: Indian Pharmacopoeia Commission (IPC) is a statutory body under the Ministry of Health & Family Welfare that sets drug quality standards and publishes the Indian Pharmacopoeia
prelims.why_important: IPC's statutory status and parent ministry are basic facts likely to appear in institution-based questions.

prelims.point: IPC launched its first-ever Indian Pharmacopoeia Phytochemical Reference Standards (IPPRS) and Indian Pharmacopoeia Botanical Reference Standards (IPBRS) at this conclave, covering compounds like Andrographolide, Capsaicin, Eugenol and plants like Tinospora cordifolia, Bacopa monnieri, Ocimum sanctum
prelims.why_important: This is the specific 'first-ever' milestone the release announces, a likely fact-based prelims trigger.

prelims.point: Reference standards (like IPPRS/IPBRS) are benchmark substances used by laboratories to verify identity, purity and potency of drugs/herbal ingredients
prelims.why_important: Understanding what a 'reference standard' means helps distinguish it from related terms like pharmacopoeial monograph in objective questions.

prelims.point: NIPER (National Institute of Pharmaceutical Education and Research) Guwahati hosted IPC's first Northeast regional conclave
prelims.why_important: NIPER institutions and their locations are occasionally tested as part of pharma education infrastructure questions.

mains.point: Standardisation of phytopharmaceuticals bridges traditional medicinal knowledge (Ayurveda, Siddha, Unani) with modern evidence-based regulatory science, aiding mainstreaming of herbal medicine
mains.theme: Integrating traditional medicine with modern healthcare
mains.analytical_use: Useful for answers on mainstreaming AYUSH/traditional medicine into evidence-based healthcare systems and associated regulatory challenges.

mains.point: Lack of standardisation and reference benchmarks has historically caused adulteration and inconsistent quality in herbal products, a gap these new standards address
mains.analytical_use: Can support answers on challenges in India's herbal/pharmaceutical quality regulation and government responses to address them.

mains.point: Decentralising standardisation efforts to biodiversity-rich Northeast India via regional institutions signals an attempt to leverage regional traditional knowledge and expertise
mains.analytical_use: Relevant for questions on leveraging India's biodiversity and regional knowledge systems for pharmaceutical innovation and drug discovery.
